screens.title: Decentralized Storage (IPFS & Filecoin)
screens.subtitle: How content addressing, CIDs, and an incentive layer solve on-chain storage limits

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn why blockchains avoid storing large files, and how decentralized storage systems like IPFS and Filecoin fill that gap. We begin by clarifying the core limitation: blockchains are optimized for small, consensus-critical data, not heavy media or large documents. Then you'll see how IPFS gives every piece of content a unique content identifier that guarantees immutability and verifiability. Next, we'll connect that to Filecoin, which provides payments and contracts so data remains persistently hosted for the period you need. Finally, you'll follow a practical DApp pattern that stores only a CID on-chain while the actual file lives on IPFS, and we'll walk through an example upload and retrieval flow using a web3. storage client library. By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to explain content addressing, generate and use CIDs, reason about availability and pinning, and make choices about privacy and encryption before uploading. Think about one concrete use case: storing an NFT image off-chain and saving its CID on-chain to keep gas costs low while preserving integrity.

keyIdea.title: Store references, not large files
keyIdea.text: Use content-addressed storage (IPFS) to hold files off-chain and store CIDs on-chain. Use Filecoin when you need guaranteed, paid persistence.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Decentralized Storage

Decentralized Storage (IPFS & Filecoin)

Understand content addressing, CIDs, and how an economic layer ensures persistent off-chain storage for DApps.

Why this matters

Blockchains are expensive for large files. Using content-addressed storage lets you keep data integrity while avoiding huge gas costs and blockchain bloat.

Orientation

You will learn practical integration, how to generate CIDs, and when to rely on pinning or Filecoin for persistence.

Quick takeaway

Keep large content off-chain, save immutable CIDs on-chain, and use an economic layer when persistence matters.

On-chain reference
Store the CID in your smart contract to link immutable data without the gas cost of the file.
Content ID

Persistence

screens.title: Why large files don't belong on-chain
screens.subtitle: Cost, consensus, and network health

narration.text: Blockchains prioritize consensus and immutability, not bulk storage. Storing a large file directly on a blockchain requires every node to include that data in their replicated state, which increases storage and synchronization costs for the entire network. That translates into high gas fees for the developer and slower node sync times for users. A concrete example: saving a high-resolution image on Ethereum would cost far more than storing only a small metadata hash. This is the practical reason DApps store only a reference to large files on-chain. A common misconception is to assume that because smart contracts can store bytes they should store full assets; in reality, storing a hash is sufficient to prove integrity and link to off-chain content. When designing a DApp, consider what must be immutable and globally verifiable, and keep only that on-chain. The takeaway is a simple design pattern: on-chain for proofs and state, off-chain for bulky assets; link them with content identifiers. Ask yourself: which parts of your app need the global guarantees of the blockchain, and which parts can live in a decentralized file system?

keyIdea.title: On-chain = proofs, not files
keyIdea.text: Keep only small, consensus-critical data on-chain; store large assets off-chain and reference them with cryptographic hashes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Why large files don't belong on-chain
Core Concept

Cost, consensus, and network health

Blockchains force every node to process and store on-chain data. Large files multiply storage needs and slow synchronization.

  • Gas costs grow with data size, making large on-chain writes expensive.
  • Node operators bear long-term storage and sync burdens when large files are included.
  • Keeping only references on-chain preserves immutability while avoiding bloat.
Concrete example
Store an NFT image off-chain and place its CID on-chain to avoid huge gas costs for the image itself.
Common mistake
Treating smart contracts as general-purpose storage instead of as anchors for proofs and references.
Design pattern

Reference pattern

// Pattern: store CID on-chain
struct Asset {
  address owner;
  string cid; // content identifier for off-chain file
}

// Smart contract retains small, verifiable reference only
Key Takeaway

Use the chain for authoritative references and proofs; delegate bulky storage to decentralized file systems.

screens.title: What is IPFS and how content addressing works
screens.subtitle: Content-based addressing, CIDs, and immutability

narration.text: IPFS is a peer-to-peer protocol for storing and sharing files in a distributed file system. Its key shift from the web is addressing by content instead of location: when you add a file to IPFS, the system computes a cryptographic hash of the file's bytes and returns a Content Identifier, or CID. That CID uniquely represents that exact content. If the content changes, the CID changes, which enforces immutability by design. A concrete example: save a text file that reads "Hello IPFS" and receive a CID; anyone fetching that CID will get precisely those bytes. This makes IPFS excellent for verifiable off-chain storage linked from a blockchain. A common misconception is to assume IPFS guarantees permanent hosting. It does not inherently persist files indefinitely unless nodes pin them or an incentive layer stores them. That difference is where Filecoin or pinning services enter the picture. Core practical implications: CIDs let you verify integrity, support deduplication across nodes that already hold identical content, and enable censorship resistance because any node with the content can serve it. Consider how an NFT metadata CID proves the exact metadata file regardless of which host serves it.

keyIdea.title: IPFS = content first
keyIdea.text: IPFS returns a CID from file contents. CIDs guarantee immutability and allow any node holding the file to serve it.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › What is IPFS
Definition

Content-based addressing, CIDs, and immutability

IPFS stores and retrieves content by its cryptographic hash. The resulting CID is a self-describing identifier for the exact bytes you added.

  • CIDs change if any byte of the content changes.
  • Multiple nodes can serve the same CID; the network finds peers that have the content.
  • IPFS supports chunking large files into content-addressed blocks for efficient distribution.
Concrete example
Upload a small text file and receive a CID. Later anyone can verify the file's integrity by matching its bytes to the CID.
Misconception
IPFS alone doesn't promise permanence; content must be pinned or placed on an incentive network for long-term availability.
How CIDs help
  1. Integrity: CID ties to exact bytes.
  2. Deduplication: identical content shares a CID across the network.
  3. Censorship resistance: any peer with the content can respond to requests.
// Example: content → hash → CID
"Hello IPFS"  —>  cryptographic hash  —>  CID (immutable identifier)
Reflect: If a file changes, do you want the old reference to still exist? IPFS makes that explicit by changing the CID.

screens.title: How IPFS distributes and retrieves content
screens.subtitle: Chunking, DHT lookup, and peer retrieval

narration.text: When you add a file to IPFS, the file is broken into smaller content-addressed blocks and each block is hashed. These blocks are advertised to the network through a distributed hash table, which maps CIDs to the peers that can serve them. When a client requests a CID, IPFS looks up peers that announced they host those blocks, and it fetches the content from whichever peer responds. A concrete scenario: a 10-megabyte image is chunked into blocks; each block gets a hash, and any node that stores the blocks can return them when asked by CID. This design enables efficient parallel retrieval and resilience: if one node is offline, another node with the same blocks can still serve the data. A common misconception is to imagine a single canonical server for every CID. In reality, IPFS is peer-to-peer: any node that holds the content can serve it. From a developer perspective, understanding how chunking and the DHT work helps you reason about retrieval latency, caching, and why pinning matters. Key takeaway: IPFS makes files retrievable from multiple hosts by mapping content hashes to peer providers, enabling resilience and redundancy without central servers.

keyIdea.title: Chunks + DHT + peers
keyIdea.text: IPFS splits files into hashed blocks, records providers in a DHT, and retrieves blocks from any peer that hosts them.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › IPFS distribution
Process Flow

Chunking, DHT lookup, and peer retrieval

Files are split into blocks, each block hashed. Providers announce which CIDs they hold into the DHT so others can find them.

  • Chunking enables parallel downloads and efficient distribution.
  • The DHT maps content identifiers to peers that host the data.
  • Clients fetch blocks from whichever peers respond first, improving resilience.
Concrete scenario
A multi-megabyte file is chunked; nodes with any chunk can supply it, so availability increases as more peers host the blocks.
Developer implications
  1. Pin blocks you care about to prevent garbage collection.
  2. Expect variable latency depending on which peers respond and network propagation.
  3. Design for reassembly of chunks when retrieving large objects.
Pro tip

Pin the root CID of important files and consider replication across multiple pinning providers to reduce single-provider availability risk.

screens.title: Pinning and persistence
screens.subtitle: Why pinning matters and how services help

narration.text: IPFS does not automatically keep content forever; nodes can garbage collect unpinned data. Pinning is the explicit operation that tells an IPFS node to retain a copy of a file and its blocks. For many developers, relying on a local node alone is insufficient; you need a pinning service or an incentive network to ensure availability. Services such as managed pinning providers will keep files pinned for you, reducing the operational burden. A practical sequence looks like this: upload a file to IPFS, get a CID, then instruct a pinning service or run a node to pin that CID. A common trap is assuming that uploading once to IPFS via a gateway guarantees permanence. Without pinning or paying for storage, the file could disappear if no peers decide to keep it. The core takeaway is that pinning provides availability but not an economic guarantee. If your application requires contractual, long-term storage, the next step is to use Filecoin or similar incentive layers which accept payment to store data for a specified duration. Think about pinning as a retention command and Filecoin as the paid contract that backs retention with incentives.

keyIdea.title: Pin to persist
keyIdea.text: Pinning ensures nodes retain content; use pinning services or Filecoin when you need persistent storage guarantees.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Pinning and persistence
Core Concept

Why pinning matters and how services help

Pinning tells a node to keep a copy of a CID's blocks and prevents garbage collection. Without pinning, content availability is opportunistic.

  • Pin locally if you manage your own node, or use a pinning provider for convenience.
  • Pinning ensures availability but is not an economic guarantee against content loss if a provider fails.
  • Combine pinning with replication across providers to reduce risk.
Workflow
  1. Upload file via client → receive CID.
  2. Pin CID to your node or a provider to retain content.
  3. Optionally, purchase Filecoin storage for contractual persistence.
Concrete example
Use web3.storage to upload and automatically pin files for a managed retention period, simplifying availability management.
Misconception
Uploading through a gateway is not the same as pinning; gateways may not retain content indefinitely for you.

screens.title: IPFS vs Filecoin: roles and trade-offs
screens.subtitle: Content addressing versus storage marketplace

narration.text: IPFS and Filecoin are complementary rather than competing. IPFS provides the protocol for content addressing and peer-to-peer transfer: you add content, receive a CID, and peers can fetch the content. Filecoin adds an economic layer where storage providers commit to storing data in exchange for payment, creating enforceable storage deals for a specified duration. A concrete contrast: IPFS without pinning offers a discovery and retrieval mechanism but not guaranteed long-term retention; Filecoin allows you to pay storage providers to retain your data over an agreed period. A common misunderstanding is to treat Filecoin as necessary for every IPFS use. In many DApps a pinning provider or web3. storage is sufficient, especially during development or for non-critical data. The trade-offs are cost, operational overhead, and contractual guarantees: Filecoin introduces payments and verifiable proofs of storage, while IPFS provides decentralization, deduplication, and content integrity. Practical implication: choose IPFS for content addressing and quick sharing; choose Filecoin when you need paid, verifiable persistence and are prepared to integrate storage deals into your workflow. The key question: do you need a contractual promise that the content will persist for months or years?

keyIdea.title: Complementary layers
keyIdea.text: Use IPFS for content addressing and distribution; use Filecoin when you require paid, enforced storage agreements for long-term persistence.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › IPFS vs Filecoin
IPFS

Content addressing & distribution

  • Addresses files by content hash (CID).
  • Peers that have content can serve it; resilient and decentralized.
  • Does not guarantee long-term hosting by itself.
Example use
Share immutable metadata for an NFT and let collectors fetch the content by CID.
Filecoin

Incentive layer for persistence

  • Market-based storage where providers accept payment to store data.
  • Offers verifiable proofs of storage for the duration of the deal.
  • Introduces cost and contract management to ensure longevity.
Example use
Pay storage providers to keep archival data available for a guaranteed period.
Key Takeaway

Choose IPFS for integrity and distribution, and add Filecoin when you require paid, verifiable persistence.

screens.title: Integrating web3.storage into a DApp
screens.subtitle: Client setup, token handling, and upload flow

narration.text: A practical integration path uses a managed client library to upload files to IPFS and pin them via a service. In our example we use a web3. storage-style client. First, generate an A P I token on the provider and keep it secret in your environment; never hard-code it into source visible to users. Next, initialize the client with the token and prepare an upload method that accepts a file, calls the client's put method, and returns a root CID. A concrete example: the client puts an array containing the file and returns a rootCid value; you then store that CID on-chain or in your app state. A common mistake is exposing the A P I token in client-side code that ships to browsers; instead use a server-side signing service or environment variables that are never committed. When implementing the upload flow, include retries and clear user feedback: show an uploading state, the returned CID, and instructions for storing or sharing that CID. The takeaway: the library abstracts IPFS and pinning details, but security practices around tokens and careful error handling remain your responsibility. Reflect: how will you keep tokens secret while allowing user uploads?

keyIdea.title: Client + secret token
keyIdea.text: Use a managed client to upload and receive a CID; protect API tokens and handle errors and retries carefully.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Integrating web3.storage
Code Walkthrough

Client setup, token handling, and upload flow

Initialize a web3.storage client with a secret token stored in environment configuration. Use the client's put method to upload files and receive a root CID.

// Pseudocode inspired by the example
const client = new Web3Storage({ token: process.env.WEB3_STORAGE_TOKEN })
const rootCid = await client.put([file], { name: file.name, maxRetries: 3 })
// rootCid is a CID string you can store on-chain
Practical notes
  • Keep the API token secret; prefer server-side storage or ephemeral upload endpoints.
  • Use retries and show clear status messages to the user during uploads.
  • Validate file sizes and types before attempting an upload.
Example flow
User selects file → app calls upload endpoint → server or client library returns CID → store CID in smart contract or database.

screens.title: Upload code pattern (DecentralizedStorage.jsx)
screens.subtitle: File selection, client.put, and handling the returned CID

narration.text: Let's walk through the upload pattern from the provided component. The typical steps are selecting a file, initializing the web3. storage client, calling put with an array of files, and receiving a root CID. In the example flow the code initializes state values for file and status, and then calls client. put([selectedFile]) with retry options. The returned rootCid is converted to a string and displayed to the user so it can be stored or referenced. A concrete example: the user selects a small text file named test. txt; the upload returns a CID like bafy... that the app shows. A common pitfall is assuming put will always succeed immediately; you should handle exceptions and provide user feedback about retries or failures. Also be mindful about storing the token in client-side code. If you need browser-based uploads, implement a short-lived server-signed token or use a backend that performs the upload for you. The takeaway: the put method abstracts IPFS and pinning layers, letting you focus on UX and secure token handling. After getting a CID, plan how your smart contract or metadata store will reference it.

keyIdea.title: Upload pattern
keyIdea.text: Select file → client.put → receive root CID → display/store CID; always handle errors and protect tokens.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Upload code pattern
Code Walkthrough

File selection, client.put, and returned CID

// Simplified upload pattern
const client = new Web3Storage({ token: process.env.WEB3_STORAGE_TOKEN })
async function uploadFile(file){
  if(!file) throw new Error('no file')
  const rootCid = await client.put([file], { name: file.name, maxRetries: 3 })
  // rootCid.toString() is the CID to store or share
  return rootCid.toString()
}
Notes & checklist
  • Validate file size and type before calling upload.
  • Show upload progress and final CID to the user.
  • Handle exceptions and implement retries for transient errors.
Security reminder
Do not embed long-lived API tokens in client shipping code. Use short-lived tokens or server uploads when possible.

screens.title: Retrieval flow and error handling
screens.subtitle: Using a CID to fetch files and handling missing content

narration.text: Retrieving content by CID is straightforward in principle: call the client's get method with the CID, check the response status, then read the returned files. In practice you must handle missing content, network errors, and the possibility that no files are returned for a CID. A concrete example: after uploading test. txt and storing the CID, a retrieval call returns a response with a files list; reading the first file as text yields the original content. If the response indicates the CID is unavailable, inform the user and consider requesting the content from alternative gateways or checking your pin status. A common misconception is to assume that any CID you generate will always be resolvable by any gateway; availability depends on which nodes have pinned the content. For robust UX, implement explicit status messages: fetching, not found, network error, or success with content. Log retrieval attempts and offer guidance for re-upload or pinning if content is missing. The takeaway: retrieval depends on network availability and pinning; design your app to surface clear recovery options when content is not found. Retrieval flow and error handling means call client.get(cid), check response.ok, read files when present, and handle missing or error cases with clear recovery steps.. In practical terms, using a cid to fetch files and handling missing content. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Robust retrieval
keyIdea.text: Call client.get(CID), check response.ok, read files when present, and handle missing or error cases with clear recovery steps.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Retrieval flow
Code Walkthrough

Using a CID to fetch files and handle missing content

// Retrieval pseudocode
const res = await client.get(cid)
if(!res.ok){
  // handle HTTP-like status and inform user
}
const files = await res.files()
if(files.length === 0){
  // no files for this CID — ask user to pin or re-upload
}
const file = files[0]
const content = await file.text() // or blob/stream for binary
Best practices
  • Report clear status: fetching, not found, failed, or success.
  • Offer recovery: re-upload, check pinning provider, or use alternative gateway.
  • Log attempts for debugging and audits.
Concrete example
After receiving a CID, attempt retrieval and display the result. If missing, guide the user to re-pin or re-upload.

screens.title: Security and availability considerations
screens.subtitle: Encryption, public CIDs, and practical trade-offs

narration.text: When using decentralized storage, security and availability require explicit attention. CIDs are public: anyone with a CID can retrieve the content unless you encrypt it first. For private data you must encrypt before uploading and manage keys securely. Another important consideration is availability: pinning or using Filecoin addresses persistence differently — pinning maintains copies, Filecoin pays providers to store data for a time. A concrete practice is to encrypt sensitive payloads locally, then upload the encrypted blob to IPFS and store the CID and key management metadata separately in a secure key store. A common mistake is to rely on obfuscation or private gateways alone for privacy; content can leak if the CID is exposed. For availability, consider redundancy: pin across multiple providers or add Filecoin deals for long-term retention. The takeaway: treat IPFS as a content-addressed store that requires your security decisions on privacy and your operational choices for availability. Ask yourself: which data requires encryption, and what level of persistence must you buy or pin for your application? Security and availability considerations means encrypt sensitive data before upload; pin or buy storage on filecoin for availability; choose based on threat and retention needs.. In practical terms, encryption, public cids, and practical trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Encrypt then upload; pin to persist
keyIdea.text: Encrypt sensitive data before upload; pin or buy storage on Filecoin for availability; choose based on threat and retention needs.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Security & Availability
Process

Encryption, public CIDs, and trade-offs

CIDs reveal nothing about content by themselves, but anyone with the CID can fetch the file. Encrypt sensitive content before upload and manage keys carefully.

  • Encrypt on the client; store decryption keys separately and securely.
  • Use pinning providers or Filecoin to meet retention requirements.
  • Audit and log who requests CIDs where privacy matters.
Checklist
  • Does the data require encryption before upload?
  • Is pinning enough, or is a Filecoin contract required?
  • How will you store and rotate encryption keys safely?
Example
Encrypt metadata client-side, upload encrypted blob to IPFS, pin it, and store the CID and key reference separately.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These are the essential concepts to retain: first, blockchains are not suitable for large bulk storage — store only proofs and references on-chain. Second, IPFS uses content addressing to generate CIDs, which provide verifiable immutability and enable any node with the content to serve it. Third, pinning ensures nodes retain data, but pinning alone does not create an economic guarantee of long-term storage. Fourth, Filecoin is an incentive layer where storage providers accept payment and verifiable proofs to commit to preserving data for a period. Fifth, when integrating decentralized storage, secure your A P I tokens, consider encrypting private content before upload, and implement robust error handling and pinning policies. These ideas form a practical architecture: upload to IPFS, pin or pay for persistence, and record the CID on-chain to connect your smart contract logic with off-chain assets. Reflect on which combination of pinning, encryption, and paid persistence matches your application's requirements.

keyIdea.title: Essential summary
keyIdea.text: Use IPFS for content addressing, pin or use Filecoin for persistence, and keep large files off-chain while referencing them with CIDs on-chain.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Key Concepts

Key Concepts

Decentralized Storage
Off-chain storage distributed across peers, offering resilience and censorship resistance.
IPFS & CIDs
Content addressing returns a cryptographic CID that uniquely identifies the uploaded bytes.
Filecoin
An economic storage network that pays providers to store data for specified durations.
Summary takeaway

Design your DApp to store small proofs on-chain, put bulk content on IPFS, pin or pay for persistence, and encrypt private data before upload.

narration.text: Keep these three reminders close as you build: first, content addressing via IPFS and CIDs gives you immutable references you can store on-chain, preserving integrity without the cost of storing files on the blockchain. Second, pinning preserves availability in the short to medium term; for contractual, long-term guarantees use Filecoin or a similar paid persistence service. Third, treat CIDs as public pointers: encrypt sensitive data before uploading and manage keys responsibly. Each decision—pin or pay, encrypt or expose—should map to your application's threat model and retention needs. Before you finish, ask: which data in your app must be globally verifiable, and which can be kept private and encrypted off-chain? What to Remember means cids prove content; pin to keep it alive; pay for guaranteed storage; encrypt private data before upload.. In practical terms, three compact concept cards. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › What to Remember

What to Remember

CID permanence
A CID ties directly to content bytes; change the content and you get a new CID.
Pinning vs Payment
Pinning keeps content available; Filecoin pays providers for verifiable, time-bound storage.
Encrypt before upload
Anyone with a CID can fetch content, so encrypt private data client-side before uploading.
Final takeaway

Design: on-chain for proofs, IPFS for distribution, pin or pay for persistence, and encrypt for privacy.
